cards.name: Ground speed taken from the walk cycle
cards.summary: Horizontal speed is not a fixed number: each frame the current leg animation's root translation is measured and turned into a speed, so animation edits change movement.
cards.behavior: While the player is on foot the game reads the total root translation of the active leg animation and divides it by that animation's own duration, then multiplies by a tuning constant. The result is applied to a force accumulator that is converted to velocity and damped every frame, so a heavier character animation really does walk more slowly and a fast one really does cover ground faster. Airborne branches use hard-coded scales instead of reading the animation: a forward jump uses 7.9, sideways jumps 2.6, a backward jump 0.8 and a jump from standing 0.2, all divided by 1000, while levitating without grip uses 0.875. Horizontal velocity is damped by a per-millisecond factor taken from frame time, and speeds below one thousandth of a unit per millisecond are snapped to zero so the player settles instead of creeping. A speed multiplier from buffs and gear scales the integrated frame time rather than the target speed, and the whole movement step is subdivided so a slow frame runs several sub-steps while a jump is in flight.

constants.name: default impulse scale
constants.unit: impulse magnitude numerator, divided by 1000 to give world units per millisecond of frame time

constants.name: animation-derived speed factor
constants.unit: world units per millisecond of frame time, per unit of animation translation divided by animation duration

constants.name: forward jump impulse scale
constants.unit: impulse numerator divided by 1000, used while the jump animation plays and forward is held

constants.name: horizontal damping
constants.unit: fraction of horizontal speed removed per millisecond of frame time (about 30 % lost on a 33.3 ms step)

constants.name: target movement step
constants.unit: sub-steps per second of reference frame time (reference step is 1000 divided by 30 milliseconds)

constants.name: fixed movement sub-step
constants.unit: milliseconds per movement sub-step while jumping

constants.name: maximum frame time
constants.unit: milliseconds of frame time accepted before it is clamped

constants.name: resting speed threshold
constants.unit: world units per millisecond, below which horizontal velocity is zeroed

capabilities: velocity damping with a settling threshold

cards.name: Scripted jump arc with input buffer
cards.summary: The rise of a jump is a timed vertical ramp of a fixed height, and a jump press is remembered briefly so it fires as soon as the player is eligible.
cards.behavior: A jump press is stamped with the current time and only honoured if the movement code reaches it within 350 milliseconds, which is the input buffer. Before the jump is accepted the game briefly restores the full standing capsule and probes the space above the head; if that probe is blocked the press is dropped and the crouch state is kept, so the player cannot jump out from under a low ceiling. The ascent is not physics at all: over 200 milliseconds the vertical target is moved upward by a cumulative 130 world units, with vertical velocity forced to zero during the rise so no impulse carries over. Once the ramp reaches its end the jump switches to a descending phase, gravity is allowed to act again and the fall timer starts. A hop chained straight after a landing only gets half of the forward impulse, recovering linearly to full over the following 300 to 600 milliseconds, which stops bunny-hopping from being the fastest way across a room.

constants.name: jump input buffer
constants.unit: milliseconds between the stored jump press and the movement step that honours it

constants.name: jump rise duration
constants.unit: milliseconds of the scripted upward ramp

constants.name: jump rise height
constants.unit: world units climbed over the whole rise ramp (standing player capsule is 170 units tall)

constants.name: chained jump impulse penalty
constants.unit: fraction of normal jump impulse for the first 300 ms after a jump ends

constants.name: jump penalty recovery window
constants.unit: milliseconds after a jump ends before the impulse multiplier is fully restored

constants.name: head clearance sample offset
constants.unit: world units of forward offset per probe ring when testing whether a jump fits

cards.name: Fall damage above a drop threshold
cards.summary: A fall only hurts once it passes 400 world units, and damage grows linearly beyond that at one point per 15 units of extra drop.
cards.behavior: When the player leaves firm ground the game records the height at the start of the fall and starts a falling flag once downward speed passes a threshold, so walking down a slope is not treated as a fall. On the frame the player lands, the drop height is the current position minus the recorded start height. Anything at or below 400 world units costs nothing; the portion above 400 is divided by 15 and applied to the player and separately to carried equipment. The same threshold and divisor appear again in the branch that ends a fall early because the capsule could not move, and that path re-averages the recorded height so a series of small blocked drops does not compound into one large hit. An unsupported move terminates the fall immediately and zeroes horizontal velocity, so sliding off a ledge stops the player rather than launching them.

constants.name: free fall drop
constants.unit: world units of drop that cause no damage (standing capsule is 170 units tall)

constants.name: fall damage divisor
constants.unit: world units of drop per point of damage beyond the free fall drop

constants.name: falling trigger speed
constants.unit: world units per millisecond of downward velocity, divided by the 33.3 ms reference step, before a fall is armed

capabilities: separate equipment wear from the same fall

cards.name: Crouch and levitate capsule heights
cards.summary: One capsule with three height offsets: standing, crouching and levitating, each switched only after the space has been re-probed.
cards.behavior: The player is a single vertical cylinder with a radius of 52 world units whose height offset is measured downward from the eye position. Standing uses 170 units, crouching 120 and levitation 220, so crouching shortens the body and levitation stretches it. Entering a crouch does not shorten the capsule immediately: the crouch-start animation plays first and only when it reports its end does the capsule shrink, which prevents the player from snapping under a ledge in one frame. Standing back up plays the reverse animation and blocks movement input until it finishes. Levitation works the other way: the taller capsule is tested before it is applied, and if the taller body would intersect geometry the spell is cancelled instead of leaving the player embedded. A forced stand, such as a levitation ending while crouched, is suppressed while crouched and the crouch state is preserved.

constants.name: player capsule radius
constants.unit: world units

constants.name: standing height offset
constants.unit: world units measured downward from the eye position

constants.name: crouching height offset
constants.unit: world units measured downward from the eye position

constants.name: levitating height offset
constants.unit: world units measured downward from the eye position

constants.name: crouch auto-stand ceiling check
constants.unit: world units of capsule height below which the game looks for room to stand up

capabilities: one capsule with three stance heights
levitation cancelled when the taller body does not fit

cards.name: Stepped capsule sweep with angular slide
cards.summary: Movement is advanced in 40-unit steps; when a step is blocked, the mover sweeps the intended direction left and right in fixed angular increments until it finds a direction that clears.
cards.behavior: A move from the current position to the desired position is split into segments no longer than 40 world units, with a hard cap of 100 segments so a single huge displacement cannot hang the frame. Each segment is applied to a copy of the capsule and validated; the copy is kept when it is free. If validation fails and the move has a vertical component the raw vertical slide is tried first, which is what lets a climbing player inch up a wall while pressing into it. Otherwise the code searches for a slide: at each increment it rotates the intended horizontal direction by that much to the right and by the same amount to the left, tests both, and stops at the first increment where either side validates, preferring the smaller deflection when both do. It steps 10 degrees at a time out to 70 degrees for the player's easy-sliding path (finer, smoother wall sliding) and 30 degrees at a time out to 90 degrees for other movers. A global flag records whether the direct path succeeded, so callers can tell a clean move from a deflected one.

constants.name: player sweep step
constants.unit: world units of movement per validated sub-step

constants.name: segment cap
constants.unit: sub-steps per move before the loop gives up

constants.name: easy slide angular increment
constants.unit: degrees per slide attempt when the mover is flagged for easy sliding

constants.name: default slide angular increment
constants.unit: degrees per slide attempt for movers without the easy-sliding flag

capabilities: angular slide search on blocked moves

cards.name: Climbing budget and ledge rejection
cards.summary: Ledges are climbable only within a per-second climbing budget and only up to a fixed penetration depth; deeper steps stop the climb outright.
cards.behavior: When a blocked capsule would have to rise over geometry, the game measures the vertical penetration it would have to swallow and converts it into a climbing cost scaled by the horizontal distance travelled, so shallow slopes are cheap and vertical faces are expensive. That cost is charged against a climbing budget capped at 12 units per second and decaying in real time. If the requested penetration is deeper than 55 world units the budget is immediately set to its maximum and the move is refused, which turns a wall into a hard stop while a low step is still free. Both slide directions are walked at each angular increment and every failed attempt restores the budget it spent, so only the direction that is finally accepted is charged. The budget therefore lets a player angle into a low ledge and ratchet over it while starving a straight-on push against a tall face.

constants.name: climbing budget ceiling
constants.unit: climbing cost units per second

constants.name: easy slide sweep limit
constants.unit: degrees either side of the intended direction searched when sliding the player

constants.name: ledge rejection depth
constants.unit: world units of vertical penetration that aborts a climb

constants.name: climb cost scale
constants.unit: multiplier converting vertical penetration divided by horizontal distance into climbing cost

capabilities: hard rejection of tall vertical faces
climb cost proportional to step steepness

cards.name: First-person camera and head attachment
cards.summary: A 75-degree vertical field of view, 2100 units of clip depth and a one-unit near plane, with the eye bolted to a head vertex that is clamped close to the body axis.
cards.behavior: The camera stores a focal length rather than an angle; the vertical field of view is derived from a fixed 480-unit image plane, so the default 75-degree view and a one-unit near plane give an extremely deep frustum that is clipped at 2100 world units. Users cannot drive the field of view below 10 degrees. In first person the camera position is copied from the head attachment vertex of the animated player mesh, and the horizontal offset from the body centre is clamped to 46 units so a head-bob animation cannot swing the view through a wall. Turning off view bobbing collapses the camera onto a stable cached head position instead. Looking out from a scripted camera blends position and orientation back toward the player at a fixed fraction per frame, and the external third-person fallback pulls the eye back up to 250 world units behind the player in 10-unit increments, adding a fixed 30 degrees to its pitch and stopping at the last increment that is still inside level geometry.

constants.name: default vertical field of view
constants.unit: degrees, vertical

constants.name: minimum field of view
constants.unit: degrees, vertical, enforced when a config value is loaded

constants.name: far clip depth
constants.unit: world units

constants.name: near plane distance
constants.unit: world units

constants.name: projection image plane height
constants.unit: world units of virtual image plane used to convert focal length to field of view

constants.name: eye offset clamp
constants.unit: world units of horizontal distance between the body axis and the head vertex

constants.name: third-person pullback step
constants.unit: world units per increment, up to 250 world units behind the player

constants.name: third-person pitch offset
constants.unit: degrees added to pitch while in external view

constants.name: camera blend fraction
constants.unit: fraction of the remaining angle closed per frame while blending back from a scripted camera

capabilities: focal-length camera with derived field of view
head-vertex eye attachment with a lateral clamp

cards.name: Bow draw zoom
cards.summary: Drawing a bow narrows the camera continuously over about 0.7 seconds by adding focal length, and the same ratio later scales arrow launch speed.
cards.behavior: While the bow's strike-cycle animation is playing the aim ratio grows with frame time divided by 710, clamped to one, which makes a full draw take about seven tenths of a second. The camera's focal length is increased by 177.5 times that ratio, so the picture tightens steadily rather than snapping to a zoom level, and the zoom decays the same way when the cycle ends. The ratio is also read at release: arrow speed is the larger of the ratio plus 0.3 and 0.9, and the downward gravity term is 0.0002 scaled by one minus the ratio, so a half-drawn arrow leaves slower and drops noticeably while a full draw flies nearly flat.

constants.name: full draw time
constants.unit: milliseconds of animation cycle per unit of aim ratio

constants.name: zoom focal gain
constants.unit: world units of focal length added at a full draw

constants.name: maximum aim ratio
constants.unit: clamp applied to the accumulated aim ratio per update

constants.name: minimum arrow speed
constants.unit: world units per millisecond of frame time at release

constants.name: partial draw gravity
constants.unit: world units per millisecond squared, scaled by one minus the aim ratio

capabilities: aim ratio shared between camera and projectile
unfinished draws fly slower and drop

cards.name: Melee charge and release
cards.summary: Holding attack winds the swing up; the fraction of the weapon's aim time that has elapsed becomes both the damage multiplier and the gate on the audible strike grunt.
cards.behavior: Attack is a two-stage gesture. Pressing attack starts the wind-up animation and sets the aim timer running; holding keeps the swing in its loop animation and the timer keeps accumulating frame time. Releasing the button fires the strike and stops the timer. The elapsed aim time is divided by the weapon's full aim time and clamped between 0.1 and 1.0, so even a tap produces a tenth of the damage rather than nothing. The full aim time is taken from the weapon's aim-time modifier in milliseconds, floored at 1500, then reduced by 20 milliseconds per point of dexterity above 10 and floored again, so a clumsy character cannot be slower than 1.5 seconds and a nimble one still cannot beat that floor. Any ratio above 0.8 also unlocks the strike shout and the backstab opportunity check.

constants.name: minimum full aim time
constants.unit: milliseconds of hold for a full charge

constants.name: dexterity aim handicap
constants.unit: milliseconds of aim time removed per point of dexterity above 10

constants.name: minimum charge ratio
constants.unit: fraction of full damage retained by a released tap

constants.name: committed strike threshold
constants.unit: fraction of the full aim time needed before the strike is treated as committed

capabilities: weapon and dexterity derived charge time

cards.name: Melee hit chance, absorption and knockback
cards.summary: Damage is attack power times charge ratio, reduced by a percentage absorb, then checked against a hit chance built from armour class minus attack power, with backstab and critical multipliers applied last.
cards.behavior: The attacker's melee damage value is multiplied by the charge ratio to give raw damage. Armour reduces it by an absorb percentage, which for the player is half of the defence skill and for creatures comes from their own absorb stat; a curse spell scales both armour class and absorb downward per level. Hit chance is 100 minus armour class minus attack power, and a random roll above that chance means a clean miss with no damage and no sound of impact. A target flagged as backstabbable, combined with a stealth roll, multiplies damage by 1.5; a successful critical roll multiplies it by another 1.5. The final damage pushes the target along the source-to-target axis, and the player receives that push through a dedicated force accumulator with separate horizontal and vertical divisors, so a heavy hit staggers the camera without sliding the player across the floor.

constants.name: player damage absorb
constants.unit: percentage points of absorb per point of defence skill

constants.name: hit chance base
constants.unit: percentage points; chance equals this minus armour class minus attack power

constants.name: backstab multiplier
constants.unit: damage factor applied once when the target is caught from behind

constants.name: critical multiplier
constants.unit: damage factor applied to a successful critical roll

constants.name: player push divisor on the attack axis
constants.unit: divisor applied to damage before adding to the player push force, per 33.3 ms reference step

constants.name: player push divisor on the vertical axis
constants.unit: divisor applied to damage for the vertical push component, per 33.3 ms reference step

capabilities: armour class versus attack power hit chance

cards.name: Hit spheres from weapon action points
cards.summary: A swing hits whatever overlaps the spheres authored on the weapon mesh, so reach and arc come from animation data rather than from a fixed range cone.
cards.behavior: Each frame a swing is active the game walks the weapon model's action points and takes only the ones named as hit points with a numeric suffix; the suffix is parsed as the sphere radius. Every hit point becomes a sphere at the animated world position of that vertex and is tested against the world. Creatures attacking the player get 15 extra world units of radius, which compensates for their coarser animation without changing the player's own reach. Anything overlapping is damaged using the closest non-hidden vertex of the target as the impact point, so sparks and blood spray appear where the weapon actually touched rather than at the target's origin. Because the spheres ride on the animated mesh, a long weapon genuinely reaches further on the frames where it is extended.

constants.name: hit point name prefix
constants.unit: naming convention on weapon action points; the numeric suffix is the sphere radius in world units

constants.name: creature hit sphere bonus
constants.unit: world units of extra hit sphere radius for attackers that are not the player

capabilities: mesh-authored weapon reach and swing arc
impact point taken from the nearest target vertex

cards.name: Arrow flight and swept hit probes
cards.summary: Arrows travel as a straight velocity with a per-frame gravity ramp, and each frame sweeps a short chain of expanding spheres along the flight direction so fast arrows cannot tunnel.
cards.behavior: A released arrow is spawned at the hand position with a direction vector scaled by its launch speed and a gravity value; the projectile stores both plus the source, the mesh, the attach vertex and a damage figure. Every update advances the position by velocity times frame time and, if gravity is non-zero, adds gravity times frame time to the vertical velocity, re-orienting the arrow mesh to the new direction so a dropping arrow visibly noses down. Collision is not a single ray: the update tests 12 spheres spaced along the arrow's local forward axis in half-unit increments of a precision value, each with the hit radius plus a small margin, and the first overlap that is not the shooter resolves the hit. A parallel ray cast against level geometry produces sparks and a surface-appropriate impact sound, and the arrow sticks where it landed instead of vanishing.

constants.name: swept probe count
constants.unit: spheres tested along the flight direction per update

constants.name: probe precision step
constants.unit: increments of the precision factor, each probe offset by 4.5 times that factor along the flight vector

constants.name: arrow damage skill scale
constants.unit: fraction of base weapon damage added per point of projectile skill plus dexterity

constants.name: launch speed bonus over aim ratio
constants.unit: world units per millisecond added to the aim ratio before the speed floor is applied

capabilities: linear flight with a per-frame gravity ramp

cards.name: Flight distance damage modifier
cards.summary: A projectile's damage is scaled by how far it has flown: half damage point-blank, full damage at 1000 units, and double beyond 2000.
cards.behavior: When a projectile connects, the game measures the straight-line distance from where it was spawned to where it currently is and turns that into a modifier. Under 2000 world units the modifier is the flight distance divided by 1000, floored at 0.5, so a shot fired from touching range does half damage and one that has covered 1000 units does full damage. Past 2000 units the modifier is simply 2, so damage keeps scaling with range instead of tapering off, which rewards leading a target across a room. The modifier multiplies the projectile's base damage along with critical and backstab terms and the target's absorb reduction, then a separate roll against armour class versus projectile damage can still cancel the hit entirely. A carried quiver's poison charge is applied on the same hit.

constants.name: reference flight distance
constants.unit: world units of travel that give a damage multiplier of exactly one

constants.name: minimum distance modifier
constants.unit: damage multiplier floor at point-blank range

constants.name: long range modifier
constants.unit: damage multiplier applied beyond twice the reference distance

constants.name: backstab multiplier on projectiles
constants.unit: damage factor applied once when the target is caught from behind

capabilities: separate armour chance check after the range modifier
poison transfer from the carried quiver

cards.name: Mouse-drawn rune recognition
cards.summary: A drawn stroke is resampled to 20 points, reduced to 19 compass directions, and matched against authored direction strings with a small tolerance.
cards.behavior: While the cast button is held the game collects raw mouse positions, capped at 200 samples so a long scribble cannot grow without bound. On release the stroke first has its corners picked out as key points, then is resampled into a fixed set of 20 positions spread across those segments by arc length, and each consecutive pair becomes one of eight compass directions derived from the screen-space angle of the segment. That gives 19 direction codes per stroke, which are compared against a table of hand-authored direction strings, one string per rune; several runes accept two alternative strings so a rounded or angular handwriting both register. Matching allows up to two direction codes to differ, which absorbs jitter and a sloppy corner without letting distinct runes collide. A recognised rune is pushed into the current spell symbol list and resets the stroke buffer; an unrecognised one clears the buffer and records the failed sequence.

constants.name: resampled stroke length
constants.unit: points the raw stroke is resampled to before direction analysis

constants.name: matching tolerance
constants.unit: direction codes that may differ between a drawn stroke and a stored rune pattern

constants.name: raw stroke sample cap
constants.unit: mouse positions retained per stroke before the buffer is reset

cards.name: Precast spell queue
cards.summary: Completed rune sequences wait in a short first-in-first-out queue; pressing cast launches the oldest entry, and no two launches can happen within one second.
cards.behavior: Recognising a full rune sequence does not cast immediately. The spell is pushed onto a small queue with its level and duration, and if the queue is already full the oldest entry is discarded to make room, so the buffer holds the three most recent invocations. Launching is a separate player action: it reads the oldest queued spell, computes the mana cost from the player's effective spell level, and only spends mana if the cost is affordable or the spell is flagged as free. A global timestamp guards the whole system so a second launch inside one second is silently ignored, which stops a player from emptying the queue in a single frame and makes each cast a deliberate beat. If the player is in combat stance when the launch fires, the stance is dropped and the casting animation restarted so the two animation layers do not fight.

constants.name: precast queue depth
constants.unit: queued spells retained; the oldest is dropped when a fourth is added

constants.name: minimum interval between launches
constants.unit: seconds of game time between two launched spells

capabilities: mana charged at launch rather than at recognition

cards.name: Magic missile volley
cards.summary: Missile count grows with spell level up to five, each extra missile is fanned out by a small random angle, and every missile detonates in an 80-unit sphere.
cards.behavior: Casting magic missile computes the number of projectiles as half of the spell level plus one, clamped between one and five, then spawns each missile from the caster's hand with the camera pitch and yaw. The first missile flies exactly where the player aims; every additional missile is jittered by up to four degrees of pitch and six degrees of yaw, giving a ragged fan rather than a tight cluster. Each missile has a six-second life with up to a second of random variation, never less than one second, and carries its own coloured light. Every frame each missile tests a ten-unit sphere against the world; on contact it explodes, dealing damage in an 80-unit radius with a base of four plus a fifth of a point per level, scaled by 0.8, typed as magical and flagged as a single-hit area effect that cannot hurt the caster. Once every missile has stopped moving the spell ends itself.

constants.name: missile count clamp
constants.unit: upper clamp on the projectile count, reached at spell level 9 and above

constants.name: missile pitch jitter
constants.unit: degrees of random pitch spread applied to every missile after the first

constants.name: missile yaw jitter
constants.unit: degrees of random yaw spread applied to every missile after the first

constants.name: missile life
constants.unit: seconds of flight before the missile expires

constants.name: missile contact radius
constants.unit: world units of the collision sphere tested each update

constants.name: explosion damage radius
constants.unit: world units

constants.name: explosion damage scale
constants.unit: multiplier applied to base damage of four plus a fifth of a point per spell level

cards.name: Fireball flight and blast
cards.summary: A fireball spends two seconds gathering in the caster's hands, then flies at a fixed speed and detonates the first thing it touches with a blast that scales with level.
cards.behavior: On launch the spell sets a six-second duration and starts a two-second creation window. During creation the ball is re-aimed at the caster's current view every frame and its speed is set for the gathering phase; once the window elapses the speed is re-fixed at the higher flight value and the ball stops following the aim, so a caster who turns after release cannot steer it. Motion uses a per-frame multiplier on the velocity rather than raw frame time, which keeps the flight visually consistent across frame rates. The contact sphere radius is twice the spell level, floored at 12 world units, so a high-level fireball is much easier to land. On contact the velocity is halved, a scorch decal and a boom are spawned, and spherical damage is applied over a radius of 30 units per level with 3 damage per level, typed fire and magical; fire protection scales the damage and everything in the blast is ignited.

constants.name: fireball duration
constants.unit: seconds of life after launch

constants.name: gathering window
constants.unit: seconds during which the ball tracks the caster and cannot be steered away from

constants.name: launch speed scale
constants.unit: velocity magnitude at launch, multiplied per frame by 0.0045 of frame time in milliseconds

constants.name: flight speed scale
constants.unit: velocity magnitude after the gathering window, multiplied per frame by 0.0045 of frame time in milliseconds

constants.name: per-frame flight multiplier
constants.unit: world units travelled per millisecond of frame time per unit of velocity scale

constants.name: minimum contact radius
constants.unit: world units of the detonation sphere, or twice the spell level if larger

constants.name: blast radius per level
constants.unit: world units of damage radius per spell level

capabilities: charge-up window before a spell is released
ignition of everything in the blast

cards.name: NPC vision cone with light gating
cards.summary: A creature sees the player only inside a 110-degree half-angle within 2000 units, and only if the player is lit above the stealth threshold, carrying a torch, or standing close.
cards.behavior: Detection measures the ground-plane angle between the creature's facing and the direction toward a point 90 world units above the player's position. Three gates must pass. First the distance must be under 2000 squared units and the player must not be invisible or dead. Second the angle between the creature's facing and the direction to the player must be within 110 degrees, measured on the ground plane. Third the player must be visible by one of three routes: the light sampled at the player's feet must exceed a stealth threshold that rises with the stealth skill, the player must be carrying a lit torch, or the player must be within 200 units where proximity overrides darkness. Touching at body radii plus 15 units with less than 200 units of vertical separation always counts, bypassing the angle test entirely. A ray against level geometry must then actually reach the player, and a hit within 25 units of the target is treated as clear. Entering and leaving visibility raise distinct events so scripts can react.

constants.name: vision half-angle
constants.unit: degrees of yaw difference around the creature's facing

constants.name: sight range
constants.unit: world units of distance beyond which the player is ignored

constants.name: proximity override range
constants.unit: world units inside which darkness does not hide the player

constants.name: contact radius slack
constants.unit: world units added to both body radii for forced detection on touch

constants.name: contact vertical tolerance
constants.unit: world units of height difference allowed for forced detection on touch

constants.name: line-of-sight near miss
constants.unit: world units by which a geometry hit may fall short of the target and still count as visible

constants.name: stealth threshold base
constants.unit: light level at zero stealth skill before any skill bonus is added

capabilities: light level compared against a stealth skill threshold
torch and proximity overrides for darkness
geometry ray confirmation with a near-miss tolerance

cards.name: Footstep noise and hearing range
cards.summary: Steps are emitted every 120 units travelled; stealth mode both quiets the step and shrinks the radius at which creatures hear it, and crouching effectively doubles the distance counted per step.
cards.behavior: Player movement accumulates travelled distance, and once that accumulator passes 120 world units a step noise is emitted and the accumulator is reduced. While crouching the travelled distance is doubled before it is added, so a crouched player produces a step roughly every 60 units of real movement, while levitation suppresses steps entirely. The emitted noise carries a volume and a falloff factor: stealth mode lowers the volume from 1.0 toward 0.94 and raises the falloff factor from 1.0 toward 4.5 in proportion to stealth skill, so a skilled sneak is barely audible past a few metres. Playing a collision sound also raises a hear event on every living creature in a trigger zone within range, carrying the distance to the noise. That range is 600 world units for anything sourced by the player and 800 for an item, multiplied by the presence value baked into the played sample and divided by the stealth-driven falloff factor, so a skilled sneak is heard from a fraction of the normal radius. When source and listener sit in different rooms the straight distance is replaced by the portal-graph room distance, so a shout through a doorway carries further than the geometry suggests. Jumps, weapon impacts, arrow hits and spell detonations all raise the same kind of event, which is why a quiet approach has to avoid combat as well as footsteps.

constants.name: step distance
constants.unit: world units of travel per footstep noise event

constants.name: crouch step distance multiplier
constants.unit: factor applied to travelled distance per step while crouched

constants.name: maximum stealth skill
constants.unit: stealth skill points used to normalise the noise reduction

constants.name: quietest step volume
constants.unit: sample volume at maximum stealth skill, down from a default of 1.0

constants.name: harshest step falloff factor
constants.unit: hearing-range divisor at maximum stealth skill, up from a default of 1.0

constants.name: step hearing range
constants.unit: world units before presence and falloff modifiers

constants.name: item hearing range
constants.unit: world units for a dropped item, before presence and falloff modifiers

capabilities: stealth skill reducing volume and range
separate hear ranges for steps and dropped items

cards.name: Pathfinding that prefers darkness
cards.summary: The anchor-graph search is ordinary A-star, but a sneaking creature adds a large surcharge for every anchor inside a lit radius, so its path drifts toward shadow.
cards.behavior: The search expands anchors from a level-built graph, skipping nodes that are flagged blocked or whose radius or height cannot fit the mover's cylinder. Edge cost is the straight distance between anchors; when the caller asks for a stealth path, the illumination cost of the destination anchor is added on top. That illumination cost sums, over every active light whose falloff reaches the anchor, a base charge multiplied by the light's intensity and average colour, and scaled down for anchors between the light's falloff start and falloff end so the edge of a pool of light is cheaper than its centre. The resulting cost can easily exceed the geometric distance, which is what bends the path around braziers instead of through them. A separate flee search inverts the goal: it walks away from a danger point until it reaches a safe radius, weighting the remaining estimate so it clears the immediate area quickly. Wandering picks a handful of random linked anchors to produce a patrol route.

constants.name: minimum anchor radius
constants.unit: world units of wander radius below which the search collapses to the current anchor instead of picking a route

constants.name: illumination cost base
constants.unit: path cost added by a fully lit anchor, scaled by light intensity and colour

constants.name: flee distance cost
constants.unit: path cost per world unit of remaining distance from the danger point while fleeing

capabilities: A-star over a prebuilt anchor graph
dedicated flee search with a safe radius

cards.name: Loose prop tumbling and settling
cards.summary: Dropped and knocked items are simulated as a cloud of mass-carrying particles under Runge-Kutta integration, bouncing off geometry with a fixed restitution and going to sleep after enough contacts.
cards.behavior: Every dynamic item carries a physics box built from its own vertices: an oriented set of particles with positions, velocities, masses and a radius derived from the mesh bounds. Launching the box rotates every particle by the throw orientation, offsets it to the launch position, and gives it a velocity proportional to the object's surface area so a big crate tumbles less wildly than a small pot, with mass rising slightly with that same surface ratio. Integration is fourth-order Runge-Kutta over a fixed small step: a constant gravity of 65 is divided by particle mass, and a damping term of 0.5 times velocity acts as drag so nothing accelerates forever. After integration the solver casts rays from each particle's old position to its new one; on a hit it reflects the velocity about the surface normal and multiplies it by separate restitution factors per axis, then restores the old position. Contacts increment a stop counter while free flight decrements it, and once the counter reaches 16 the object is put to sleep until something disturbs it, which keeps a room full of debris from costing anything.

constants.name: prop gravity
constants.unit: world units of acceleration per solver time unit, divided by particle mass before each integration step

constants.name: prop damping
constants.unit: velocity-proportional drag per solver time unit, applied by the force solver

constants.name: launch velocity scale
constants.unit: velocity multiplier per solver time unit, scaled by the object's surface-area ratio

constants.name: base particle mass
constants.unit: mass units, plus 0.1 per unit of surface-area ratio

constants.name: velocity clamp
constants.unit: velocity per solver time unit per axis, clamped before every integration step

constants.name: integration threshold
constants.unit: accumulator threshold per frame; frame time in milliseconds times 0.0055 is added each step, and a step runs only when the accumulator passes it

constants.name: sleep contact count
constants.unit: accumulated contacts before the prop is put to sleep

cards.name: Carried torch light and burn-down
cards.summary: A held torch is one dynamic point light with a 1.6 intensity, a falloff band around 280 units that flickers per frame, and a durability that drains while it is held.
cards.behavior: Equipping a torch does not add a light per torch: it fills one reserved dynamic light slot owned by the player. Every frame, while a torch is held, that light is moved to the player position, given an intensity of 1.6, a falloff start of about 280 units with a small per-frame random flicker and a falloff end another 280 units further out, and coloured from the player's torch tint with a small random darkening so the pool of light breathes rather than sitting still. The light is marked as existing with no countdown, so it lasts as long as the torch does. Durability is drained per millisecond of frame time, and when it reaches zero the torch is destroyed, the light handle is cleared and the looping sound stops. With no torch the same slot falls back to a dim flare-driven light when magic flares are active, which is why carried spells light the player's surroundings without a torch.

constants.name: torch light intensity
constants.unit: light intensity units, refreshed every frame

constants.name: torch falloff start
constants.unit: world units from the light centre where falloff begins, plus up to 20 units of per-frame flicker

constants.name: torch falloff width
constants.unit: world units between the start and the end of the falloff band

constants.name: torch burn rate
constants.unit: durability points lost per millisecond of frame time while held

constants.name: fallback flare light intensity
constants.unit: light intensity units used when magic flares supply the player's light instead of a torch

capabilities: single reusable dynamic light slot for the held torch
per-frame flicker on intensity colour and falloff
durability burn-down that destroys the torch
